name: Chapter 9: Ray Optics and Optical Instruments
description: Mirrors, refraction, total internal reflection, lenses, prisms, microscopes and telescopes with NEET/JEE-style problems

cards.term: Speed of light in vacuum: exact value and the value used in problems?
cards.definition: 2.998 × 10⁸ m/s (c = 2.99792458 × 10⁸); use 3 × 10⁸ m/s. It is the maximum speed attainable in nature

cards.term: Light is a wave, yet appears to travel in straight lines. Why?
cards.definition: Its wavelength (~ 500 nm) is tiny compared with everyday objects, so it can be treated as a ray (ray optics)

cards.term: What is a ray and what is a beam of light?
cards.definition: Ray: the straight-line path along which light travels between two points. Beam: a bundle of rays

cards.term: When does ray optics fail?
cards.definition: When the sizes of obstacles or apertures become comparable to λ: then diffraction and interference matter (Chapter 10)

cards.term: Laws of reflection?
cards.definition: ∠i = ∠r and the incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in the same plane. They hold at every point of any surface

cards.term: For a spherical mirror, what is the normal at the point of incidence?
cards.definition: The radius: the line joining the centre of curvature C to that point

cards.term: Define pole, centre of curvature, principal axis of a mirror.
cards.definition:
Pole P: geometric centre of the mirror.
Centre of curvature C: centre of the sphere it is part of.
Principal axis: the line through P and C

cards.term: State the Cartesian sign convention.
cards.definition: All distances from the pole / optical centre. Along the incident light: positive; against it: negative. Heights above the axis positive, below negative

cards.term: Sign of u, f, R for a concave mirror with a real object?
cards.definition: u < 0, f < 0, R < 0 (all measured against the incident light)

cards.term: Sign of f and R for a convex mirror?
cards.definition: Positive (focus and centre lie behind the mirror, along the direction of incident light)

cards.term: Exam trap: object distance and height for a real object in front of a mirror or lens?
cards.definition: u is always negative (object on the incident side); height h is positive if the object stands upward

cards.term: Mnemonic: signs of f for the four devices?
cards.definition: Concave mirror −, convex mirror +, convex lens +, concave lens −. Like “C-C-negative, x-x-positive” for mirrors; lenses are the opposite

cards.term: Paraxial rays: meaning?
cards.definition: Rays close to the principal axis, making small angles with it (so tan θ ≈ θ)

cards.term: Where does a parallel beam focus for a concave mirror?
cards.definition: Rays converge at the principal focus F (real)

cards.term: Where does a parallel beam focus for a convex mirror?
cards.definition: Reflected rays appear to diverge from F behind the mirror (virtual focus)

cards.term: What is the focal plane?
cards.definition: The plane through F ⟂ the axis, where a parallel beam at an angle to the axis focuses

cards.term: Relation between focal length and radius of curvature?
Derive f = R/2.
cards.definition: Ray parallel to axis hits M; ∠MCP = θ so ∠MFP = 2θ. tan θ = MD/CD, tan 2θ = MD/FD → for small θ: FD = CD/2, i.e. f = R/2

cards.term: When is an image real, and when virtual?
cards.definition: Real: rays actually converge at the point. Virtual: they only appear to diverge from it (cannot be caught on a screen)

cards.term: Which two rays are easiest to draw for a mirror?
cards.definition: (i) Parallel to axis → reflects through F. (ii) Through C → retraces its path. (iii) Through F → reflects parallel. (iv) At P → reflects with i = r

cards.term: Mirror equation?
cards.definition: \( \dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f} \) (valid for concave and convex mirrors, real and virtual images)

cards.term: Linear magnification of a mirror?
cards.definition: \( m = \dfrac{h\prime}{h} = -\dfrac{v}{u} \). m < 0: real, inverted. m > 0: virtual, erect. |m| > 1: magnified

cards.term: Derive the mirror equation (outline).
cards.definition: Similar triangles A′B′F ∼ MPF and A′B′P ∼ ABP give (B′P − FP)/FP = B′P/BP. With B′P = −v, FP = −f, BP = −u this becomes 1/v + 1/u = 1/f

cards.term: Concave mirror, virtual image: object between P and F. Nature of image?
cards.definition: Virtual, erect, magnified, behind the mirror (used in shaving mirrors)

cards.term: Convex mirror: nature of image for any object position?
cards.definition: Always virtual, erect, diminished, between P and F

cards.term: Concave mirror: position of object → image
cards.definition: At infinity: At F; real, inverted, highly diminished; Beyond C: Between F and C; real, inverted, diminished; At C: At C; real, inverted, same size; Between C and F: Beyond C; real, inverted, magnified; At F: At infinity; real, inverted, highly magnified; Between F and P: Behind the mirror; virtual, erect, magnified

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Concave mirror

Image formed for object at…?

At infinity?
Beyond C?
At C?
Between C and F?
At F?
Between F and P?
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Concave mirror

Image formed for object at…?

At infinityAt F; real, inverted, highly diminished
Beyond CBetween F and C; real, inverted, diminished
At CAt C; real, inverted, same size
Between C and FBeyond C; real, inverted, magnified
At FAt infinity; real, inverted, highly magnified
Between F and PBehind the mirror; virtual, erect, magnified

cards.term: Image formation by a concave mirror as u decreases
cards.definition: u > 2f: real, inverted, diminished, between F and C; u = 2f: same size at C; f < u < 2f: magnified, beyond C; u = f: at infinity; u < f: virtual, erect, magnified

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Concave mirror · image walk

An object walks towards a concave mirror from far away to inside F. How do the image’s position, size and nature change?

Watch the red image as the yellow object moves.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Concave mirror · image walk

An object walks towards a concave mirror from far away to inside F. How do the image’s position, size and nature change?

Far away: small real image just beyond F. As the object approaches C the image grows and moves out to C (same size).

Between C and F: image real, inverted, magnified, beyond C. At F it goes to infinity; inside F it flips to a virtual, erect, magnified image behind the mirror.

cards.term: Uses of concave and convex mirrors?
cards.definition: Concave: shaving/make-up mirrors, torches and headlights, dentists’ mirrors, solar cookers. Convex: vehicle rear-view mirrors, street lights (wide field of view)

cards.term: Why do rear-view mirrors use convex mirrors?
cards.definition: Always an erect, diminished image and a wide field of view

cards.term: Example 9.1: lower half of a concave mirror is covered. Effect on the image?
cards.definition: The whole image still forms (every point reflects), but its intensity is halved

cards.term: Example 9.2: why is the image of a phone lying along the principal axis distorted?
cards.definition: Different parts are at different u, so different magnification (longitudinal ≠ lateral). Only the part in the plane ⟂ axis keeps its size

cards.term: Position, nature, magnification (Example 9.3)
cards.definition: Case (i): v = −30 cm, m = −3; case (ii): v = +15 cm, m = +3 (virtual)

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Example 9.3 · concave mirror

Find the missing step.

Concave mirror of R = 15 cm. Object at (i) 10 cm, (ii) 5 cm. Find v, nature and m.
  1. f = −R/2 = −7.5 cm
  2. ?
  3. (ii) u = −5: 1/v = −1/7.5 + 1/5 → v = +15 cm
  4. m = −15/(−5) = +3: virtual, erect, magnified
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Example 9.3 · concave mirror

Find the missing step.

Concave mirror of R = 15 cm. Object at (i) 10 cm, (ii) 5 cm. Find v, nature and m.
  1. f = −R/2 = −7.5 cm
  2. (i) u = −10: 1/v = 1/f − 1/u = −1/7.5 + 1/10 → v = −30 cm, m = −v/u = −3 (real, inverted, magnified)
  3. (ii) u = −5: 1/v = −1/7.5 + 1/5 → v = +15 cm
  4. m = −15/(−5) = +3: virtual, erect, magnified

cards.term: Example 9.4: jogger approaches a convex side mirror (R = 2 m) at 5 m/s. How does the image speed change?
cards.definition: Image speed rises steeply as the jogger nears: 1/280, 1/150, 1/60, 1/10 m/s at 39, 29, 19, 9 m. Since v = fu/(u − f) changes ever faster near the mirror (an “objects are closer than they appear” effect)

cards.term: Teacher addition: speed of the image relative to the mirror, in terms of the object’s speed?
cards.definition: \( v_I = -\dfrac{v^2}{u^2}\,v_O \) (differentiate 1/v + 1/u = 1/f). The longitudinal magnification is m²

cards.term: Teacher addition: object at 2f from a concave mirror moves 1 cm towards it. Image position and size change?
cards.definition: Longitudinal magnification = m² = 1, so the image moves 1 cm away from the mirror (at C the image and object move equal distances)

cards.term: Teacher addition: plane mirror in this language?
cards.definition: R → ∞, so f → ∞: v = −u, m = +1 (virtual, erect, same size, as far behind as the object is in front)

cards.term: Teacher addition: a plane mirror rotates by θ. Rotation of the reflected ray?
cards.definition: 2θ (used in galvanometer lamp-and-scale arrangements)

cards.term: What is refraction?
cards.definition: Change in the direction of a ray as it passes obliquely into another transparent medium (speed changes; frequency does not)

cards.term: State Snell’s laws.
cards.definition:
(i) Incident ray, refracted ray and normal are coplanar.
(ii) \( \dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r} = n_{21} \) (constant for the pair of media and the wavelength)

cards.term: Meaning of n₂₁ and its relation to speeds?
cards.definition: Refractive index of medium 2 w.r.t. 1: \( n_{21} = \dfrac{n_2}{n_1} = \dfrac{v_1}{v_2} \)

cards.term: Absolute refractive index?
cards.definition: \( n = \dfrac{c}{v} \) (medium’s index w.r.t. vacuum); for two media: n₂₁ = n₂/n₁

cards.term: Denser medium: bending of the ray?
cards.definition: Entering a denser medium (n₂₁ > 1): ray bends towards the normal (r < i). Into a rarer medium: away (r > i)

cards.term: Optical density vs mass density?
cards.definition: Optical density is the ratio of speeds of light; not mass per volume. Turpentine has lower mass density than water but higher optical density

cards.term: Relations among n₁₂, n₂₁ and n₃₁?
cards.definition: n₁₂ = 1/n₂₁, and n₃₁ = n₃₂ × n₂₁

cards.term: What changes and what stays the same for light entering glass from air?
cards.definition: Speed and wavelength decrease (λ_m = λ/n); frequency unchanged, so colour is unchanged

cards.term: Parallel-sided glass slab: deviation and lateral shift?
cards.definition: Emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray (no deviation) but laterally shifted

cards.term: Teacher addition: lateral shift by a slab of thickness t?
cards.definition: \( d = \dfrac{t\sin(i-r)}{\cos r} \); zero for normal incidence, max as i → 90°

cards.term: Apparent depth (near-normal viewing)?
cards.definition: \( h_app = \dfrac{h_real}{n} \): a tank of depth h_real appears raised to h_real/n

cards.term: Teacher addition: apparent shift of the bottom of a tank of depth h?
cards.definition:
\( h\left(1-\dfrac{1}{n}\right) \) (raised).
For a glass slab of thickness t viewed normally: shift t(1 − 1/n) as well

cards.term: Teacher addition: an object at depth in medium 1 (n₁) seen from medium 2 (n₂). Apparent depth?
cards.definition: h_app = h × (n₂/n₁) (viewer’s medium over object’s medium). Layered media: apparent depth = Σ tᵢ/nᵢ

cards.term: Exam trap: does the apparent depth depend on how deep the observer is above the water?
cards.definition: No (for near-normal viewing). It depends only on n and real depth; oblique viewing distorts it

cards.term: What happens to a ray going from a denser to a rarer medium as i increases?
cards.definition: The refracted ray bends away from the normal until r = 90° at i = i_c; beyond that no refraction: total internal reflection

cards.term: Define the critical angle.
cards.definition: The angle of incidence in the denser medium for which the angle of refraction is 90°

cards.term: Critical angle formula?
cards.definition: \( \sin i_c = \dfrac{n_2}{n_1} = \dfrac{1}{n_{12}} \) (n₁ denser, n₂ rarer); against air: sin i_c = 1/n

cards.term: Two conditions for TIR?
cards.definition: (1) light goes from a denser to a rarer medium; (2) angle of incidence > i_c

cards.term: Critical angles with respect to air (Table 9.1)?
cards.definition: Water (1.33): 48.75°; crown glass (1.52): 41.14°; dense flint (1.62): 37.31°; diamond (2.42): 24.41°

cards.term: Why does diamond sparkle?
cards.definition: Its very small critical angle (24.4°) means light entering is totally internally reflected many times before emerging

cards.term: Difference between ordinary reflection and TIR in intensity?
cards.definition: Ordinary reflection always loses some light to transmission. TIR has no transmission: reflected intensity ≈ 100%

cards.term: Refraction to total internal reflection as i increases
cards.definition: Denser to rarer: refracted ray bends away from normal; at i = ic, r = 90°; for i > ic total internal reflection; sin ic = 1/n

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Total internal reflection · sweep

A ray goes from water to air and its angle of incidence is slowly increased. What happens to the refracted and reflected rays?

Watch the red refracted ray.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Total internal reflection · sweep

A ray goes from water to air and its angle of incidence is slowly increased. What happens to the refracted and reflected rays?

Water → air: the refracted ray bends away from the normal. At the critical angle i_c (sin i_c = 1/n = 0.75, i_c = 48.75°) it skims along the surface (r = 90°).

For i > i_c there is no refracted ray: all the light is reflected. Only possible from a denser to a rarer medium.

cards.term: Demonstrating TIR with a laser pointer and turbid water?
cards.definition: Milk makes the beam visible. Aiming it up at the surface: partial reflection and refraction; at a shallow angle: TIR (same as light along a test tube or optical fibre)

cards.term: Prism that bends light by 90°: condition on i_c?
cards.definition: A right-angled isosceles prism (45°–45°–90°) works if i_c < 45°: true for crown and flint glass

cards.term: Prism to turn light by 180° and to invert an image?
cards.definition: Two TIRs at the 45° faces reverse the beam (180°); the arrangement of Fig 9.13(c) inverts the image without changing size (binoculars, periscopes)

cards.term: Optical fibre: structure and principle?
cards.definition: Core of high n inside a cladding of lower n; light undergoes repeated TIR along the length

cards.term: Why is there little loss in an optical fibre?
cards.definition: TIR at each reflection (no transmission) and very pure quartz: > 95% of light survives 1 km

cards.term: Uses of optical fibres?
cards.definition: Telecommunication signals, endoscopy (light pipe for esophagus, stomach, intestine), decorative lamps, sensors

cards.term: Natural examples of TIR?
cards.definition: Mirage, sparkle of diamond, shine of an air bubble in water, glittering of a cracked glass

cards.term: Exam trap: a fibre has core n = 1.5 and cladding n = 1.4. What condition ensures TIR inside?
cards.definition: Angle of incidence on the core–cladding boundary must exceed i_c = sin⁻¹(1.4/1.5) ≈ 69°, i.e. the ray stays close to the axis

cards.term: Teacher addition: numerical aperture / acceptance angle of a fibre?
cards.definition: \( \sin i_{max} = \sqrt{n_{core}^2 - n_{clad}^2} \) (light entering from air within this cone is guided)

cards.term: What is a thin lens?
cards.definition: A transparent medium bounded by two surfaces (at least one spherical) whose thickness is small compared with the radii of curvature and distances

cards.term: Refraction at a single spherical surface: formula?
cards.definition: \( \dfrac{n_2}{v} - \dfrac{n_1}{u} = \dfrac{n_2 - n_1}{R} \) (light from n₁ to n₂; u, v, R with the Cartesian convention)

cards.term: Derive the formula (outline).
cards.definition: i = ∠NOM + ∠NCM, r = ∠NCM − ∠NIM (small angles). Snell: n₁i = n₂r. Substituting tan ≈ angle and signs OM = −u, MI = +v, MC = +R gives n₂/v − n₁/u = (n₂ − n₁)/R

cards.term: Single spherical refracting surface (Example 9.5)

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Example 9.5 · glass surface

Find the missing step.

Point source in air 100 cm from a spherical glass surface (n = 1.5, R = +20 cm). Find the image.
  1. n₁ = 1, n₂ = 1.5, u = −100, R = +20
  2. n₂/v − n₁/u = (n₂ − n₁)/R → 1.5/v + 1/100 = 0.5/20
  3. ?
  4. v = +100 cm: image forms 100 cm inside the glass, along the incident light
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Example 9.5 · glass surface

Find the missing step.

Point source in air 100 cm from a spherical glass surface (n = 1.5, R = +20 cm). Find the image.
  1. n₁ = 1, n₂ = 1.5, u = −100, R = +20
  2. n₂/v − n₁/u = (n₂ − n₁)/R → 1.5/v + 1/100 = 0.5/20
  3. 1.5/v = 0.025 − 0.01 = 0.015
  4. v = +100 cm: image forms 100 cm inside the glass, along the incident light

cards.term: Teacher addition: plane refracting surface (R → ∞)?
cards.definition: n₂/v = n₁/u, i.e. v/u = n₂/n₁ (this reproduces apparent depth)

cards.term: How do you get the lens formula from two spherical surfaces?
cards.definition: Image of the first surface acts as (virtual) object for the second. Adding the two equations for a thin lens gives 1/v − 1/u = (n₂/n₁ − 1)(1/R₁ − 1/R₂)

cards.term: First and second surface images for a double-convex lens?
cards.definition: First surface: real image I₁, which is a virtual object for the second surface, which forms the final image I

cards.term: Lens maker’s formula (lens of index n in air)?
cards.definition: \( \dfrac{1}{f} = (n-1)\left(\dfrac{1}{R_1} - \dfrac{1}{R_2}\right) \) (sign convention; true for concave lenses too)

cards.term: Lens maker’s formula when the lens (n₂) is in a medium (n₁)?
cards.definition: \( \dfrac{1}{f} = \left(\dfrac{n_2}{n_1} - 1\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{R_1} - \dfrac{1}{R_2}\right) \)

cards.term: Signs of R₁ and R₂ for a double convex lens? Double concave?
cards.definition: Biconvex: R₁ > 0, R₂ < 0 (so f > 0). Biconcave: R₁ < 0, R₂ > 0 (f < 0)

cards.term: Thin lens formula?
cards.definition:
\( \dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f} \) (all signs by Cartesian convention).
Note the minus sign, unlike the mirror’s plus

cards.term: Exam trap: mirror vs lens formula?
cards.definition: Mirror: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f. Lens: 1/v − 1/u = 1/f. Both m = v/u for a lens; mirror m = −v/u

cards.term: Lens magnification?
cards.definition: \( m = \dfrac{h\prime}{h} = \dfrac{v}{u} \). Negative: real, inverted. Positive: virtual, erect

cards.term: First and second principal foci?
cards.definition: F (on the source side) and F′ (other side), equidistant from the optical centre for a lens with the same medium on both sides

cards.term: Ray rules for a convex lens?
cards.definition: (i) Parallel to axis → through F′. (ii) Through the optical centre → undeviated. (iii) Through F → emerges parallel

cards.term: Ray rules for a concave lens?
cards.definition: Parallel ray appears to come from F (on the incident side); ray through optical centre undeviated; ray directed to F′ emerges parallel

cards.term: Convex lens: position of object → image
cards.definition: At infinity: At F′; real, inverted, highly diminished; Beyond 2F: Between F′ and 2F′; real, inverted, diminished; At 2F: At 2F′; real, inverted, same size; Between F and 2F: Beyond 2F′; real, inverted, magnified; At F: At infinity; real, inverted, highly magnified; Between F and O: Same side; virtual, erect, magnified (magnifier)

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Convex lens

Image for object at…?

At infinity?
Beyond 2F?
At 2F?
Between F and 2F?
At F?
Between F and O?
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Convex lens

Image for object at…?

At infinityAt F′; real, inverted, highly diminished
Beyond 2FBetween F′ and 2F′; real, inverted, diminished
At 2FAt 2F′; real, inverted, same size
Between F and 2FBeyond 2F′; real, inverted, magnified
At FAt infinity; real, inverted, highly magnified
Between F and OSame side; virtual, erect, magnified (magnifier)

cards.term: Concave lens: image for any object position?
cards.definition: Always virtual, erect, diminished, between F and the lens

cards.term: Example 9.6: how can a glass lens (n = 1.47) “disappear” in a liquid?
cards.definition: When n_liquid = 1.47, 1/f = 0, f → ∞, so it acts like a plane glass sheet. Not water (1.33); could be glycerine

cards.term: Teacher addition: a convex lens is placed in a liquid of larger index than the lens. Behaviour?
cards.definition: n₂/n₁ < 1, so the sign of f flips: it acts like a diverging lens. (Air bubble in water: a concave-behaving “lens”)

cards.term: Define power of a lens, and its unit.
cards.definition: \( P = \dfrac{1}{f} \) (f in metres); unit dioptre (D) = m⁻¹; + for convex, − for concave

cards.term: Prescription +2.5 D and −4.0 D: what lenses?
cards.definition: +2.5 D: convex, f = +40 cm. −4.0 D: concave, f = −25 cm

cards.term: Lens power, refractive index and lens in water (Example 9.7)
cards.definition: P = +2 D, n = 1.5, f in water ≈ 78.2 cm

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Example 9.7 · lens in different media

Find the missing step.

(i) f = 0.5 m: P? (ii) Biconvex R₁ = 10 cm, R₂ = −15 cm, f = 12 cm: n? (iii) A glass lens (n = 1.5) has f = 20 cm in air. Find f in water (n = 1.33).
  1. (i) P = 1/0.5 = +2 D
  2. (ii) 1/12 = (n − 1)(1/10 + 1/15) = (n − 1)/6 → n = 1.5
  3. (iii) In air: 1/20 = 0.5 (1/R₁ − 1/R₂) → (1/R₁ − 1/R₂) = 1/10
  4. ?
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Example 9.7 · lens in different media

Find the missing step.

(i) f = 0.5 m: P? (ii) Biconvex R₁ = 10 cm, R₂ = −15 cm, f = 12 cm: n? (iii) A glass lens (n = 1.5) has f = 20 cm in air. Find f in water (n = 1.33).
  1. (i) P = 1/0.5 = +2 D
  2. (ii) 1/12 = (n − 1)(1/10 + 1/15) = (n − 1)/6 → n = 1.5
  3. (iii) In air: 1/20 = 0.5 (1/R₁ − 1/R₂) → (1/R₁ − 1/R₂) = 1/10
  4. In water: 1/f = (1.5/1.33 − 1)(1/10) → f ≈ +78.2 cm (weaker lens)

cards.term: Exam trap: what happens to the focal length of a glass lens when moved from air into water?
cards.definition: It increases (about 4×): the relative index n_g/n_w = 1.13 is less than n_g/n_a = 1.5, so the lens is weaker

cards.term: Focal length of thin lenses in contact?
cards.definition: \( \dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{f_1} + \dfrac{1}{f_2} + \dots \), or P = P₁ + P₂ + … (algebraic sum)

cards.term: Magnification of a lens combination?
cards.definition: m = m₁ × m₂ × m₃ …

cards.term: Example 9.8: image position for the three-lens system f = +10, −10, +30 cm; first object at 30 cm, gaps 5 cm and 10 cm.
cards.definition: Lens 1: v₁ = 15 cm. Object for lens 2 is 10 cm beyond it (virtual): v₂ = ∞. Lens 3 gets a parallel beam, so the final image is at its focus: 30 cm right of lens 3

cards.term: Exercise 9.10: 30 cm convex lens in contact with a 20 cm concave lens. System?
cards.definition: 1/f = 1/30 − 1/20 = −1/60: diverging, f = −60 cm

cards.term: Teacher addition: two thin lenses separated by a distance d (in air)?
cards.definition:
\( \dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{f_1} + \dfrac{1}{f_2} - \dfrac{d}{f_1f_2} \).
The effective focal length depends on which side the light enters (see Exercise 9.20)

cards.term:
Teacher addition: a convex lens is cut into two halves
(a) along the axis
(b) across the axis. Focal length of each half?
cards.definition: (a) Cut along the principal axis (two thin halves): f unchanged (the intensity of the image halves). (b) Cut ⟂ to the axis: each half is a plano-convex lens with f doubled

cards.term: Teacher addition: object between two lenses, or a lens and a plane mirror behind it?
cards.definition: Use the formula lens by lens; for a mirror behind the lens, light passes the lens twice (equivalent power: 2P_lens + P_mirror)

cards.term: Prism relations for angle of deviation?
cards.definition: r₁ + r₂ = A and δ = i + e − A

cards.term: How does δ vary with the angle of incidence?
cards.definition: It falls to a minimum D_m at i = e and rises again; for a given δ (other than D_m) there are two values of i (i and e interchange)

cards.term: Condition and results at minimum deviation?
cards.definition: i = e, r₁ = r₂ = A/2; the ray inside is parallel to the base. \( D_m = 2i - A \)

cards.term: Prism formula for refractive index?
Thin prism (small A): deviation?
cards.definition: \( \delta = (n-1)A \): a thin prism does not deviate light much; independent of i for small angles

cards.term: Prism in a medium of index n₁?
cards.definition: \( n_{21} = \dfrac{n_2}{n_1} = \dfrac{\sin[(A + D_m)/2]}{\sin(A/2)} \): D_m decreases if the surrounding medium is denser

cards.term: Exam trap: a prism is placed in water. What happens to its deviation?
cards.definition: It decreases (relative index falls); Exercise 9.6: D_m falls from 40° to about 10°

cards.term: Dispersion (NCERT summary)?
cards.definition: Splitting of white light into its colours due to the different refractive indices for different wavelengths

cards.term: Teacher addition: which colour deviates most in a prism? Why?
cards.definition: Violet (shortest λ, largest n; Cauchy: n = A + B/λ²). Red deviates least, moves fastest in glass

cards.term: Teacher addition: angular dispersion and dispersive power of a thin prism?
cards.definition:
Angular dispersion: \( \delta_v - \delta_r = (n_v - n_r)A \).
Dispersive power \( \omega = \dfrac{n_v - n_r}{n_y - 1} \)

cards.term: Teacher addition: rainbow and blue sky in one line each?
cards.definition: Rainbow: dispersion + total internal reflection inside raindrops. Sky is blue and sunset red because of Rayleigh scattering ∝ 1/λ⁴

cards.term: Exercise 9.21: incidence angle so a ray just undergoes TIR on the second face (A = 60°, n = 1.524)?
Least distance of distinct vision D?
cards.definition: About 25 cm: the nearest distance at which a normal eye sees comfortably (the near point)

cards.term: What is angular magnification (magnifying power)?
cards.definition: Ratio of the angle subtended by the image to the angle subtended by the object at the near point D

cards.term: Simple microscope: what is it and how is it used?
cards.definition: A convex lens of small f held near the object (u ≤ f), giving an erect, magnified, virtual image at ≥ 25 cm

cards.term: Magnifying power of a simple microscope: image at the near point?
cards.definition: \( m = 1 + \dfrac{D}{f} \)

cards.term: Magnifying power of a simple microscope: image at infinity?
cards.definition: \( m = \dfrac{D}{f} \) (relaxed eye; one less than the near-point value)

cards.term: Derive m = 1 + D/f for the near-point image.
cards.definition: m = v/u = v(1/v − 1/f) = 1 − v/f. With v = −D: m = 1 + D/f

cards.term: How does a magnifier give angular magnification if image angle = object angle?
cards.definition: It lets you place the object much closer than 25 cm so it subtends a larger angle; without it the object must stay at D (Exercise 9.25a)

cards.term: Maximum magnification of a single simple microscope in practice?
cards.definition: About ≤ 9 for realistic f (aberrations rise as f shrinks)

cards.term: Compound microscope: parts and image nature?
cards.definition: Objective (small f, near the object): real, inverted, magnified image near the focal plane of the eyepiece, which acts as a magnifier giving a final virtual, inverted, enlarged image

cards.term: Figure 9.24 · Compound microscope
Magnification due to the objective? Tube length?
cards.definition: \( m_o = \dfrac{L}{f_o} \); L = distance between the second focus of the objective and first focus of the eyepiece (tube length)

cards.term: Magnifying power of a compound microscope, image at infinity?
cards.definition: \( m = m_o m_e = \dfrac{L}{f_o}\cdot\dfrac{D}{f_e} \)

cards.term: Magnifying power of a compound microscope, image at near point?
cards.definition: \( m = \dfrac{v_o}{|u_o|}\left(1 + \dfrac{D}{f_e}\right) \approx \dfrac{L}{f_o}\left(1 + \dfrac{D}{f_e}\right) \)

cards.term: Why must both lenses of a compound microscope have short focal lengths?
cards.definition: m ∝ 1/(f_o f_e): the objective must form a large image of a close object and the eyepiece must magnify strongly (Exercise 9.25d)

cards.term: Example: f_o = 1 cm, f_e = 2 cm, tube length 20 cm. Magnifying power (image at infinity)?
cards.definition: m = (20/1)(25/2) = 250

cards.term: Why should the eye sit at the “eye-ring” and not touching the eyepiece?
cards.definition: The eye-ring is the image of the objective formed by the eyepiece: all refracted rays pass through it, so the pupil there collects all the light (Exercise 9.25e)

cards.term: Teacher addition: how do you increase resolving power of a microscope?
cards.definition: Use a smaller λ and larger numerical aperture: \( R.P. = \dfrac{2\mu\sin\theta}{1.22\,\lambda} \) (oil immersion increases μ)

cards.term: Refracting astronomical telescope: purpose and lenses?
cards.definition: Angular magnification of distant objects. Objective: large f, large aperture; eyepiece: small f. Final image inverted

cards.term: Magnifying power of a telescope in normal adjustment (image at infinity)?
cards.definition: \( m = \dfrac{\beta}{\alpha} = \dfrac{f_o}{f_e} \); tube length f_o + f_e

cards.term: Telescope with the final image at the near point?
cards.definition: \( m = \dfrac{f_o}{f_e}\left(1 + \dfrac{f_e}{D}\right) \) and tube length f_o + u_e

cards.term: Terrestrial telescope: what is added?
cards.definition: A pair of inverting lenses (or a prism) to make the final image erect

cards.term: Two main considerations for an astronomical telescope?
cards.definition: Light-gathering power (∝ aperture area) and resolving power (∝ aperture diameter)

cards.term: Why do modern telescopes use mirrors as objectives?
cards.definition: A mirror has no chromatic aberration, is lighter, can be supported over its whole back, and is easier to make large and free of distortion

cards.term: Cassegrain telescope: layout and advantages?
cards.definition: Concave primary + convex secondary sending light through a hole in the primary: long focal length in a short tube, observer not in the way

cards.term: Figure 9.26 · Cassegrain telescope
Largest telescopes named in NCERT?
cards.definition: India’s largest: 2.34 m, Kavalur (Tamil Nadu), Cassegrain reflector. Largest lens: 1.02 m (Yerkes). Keck (Hawaii): 10 m; Mt. Palomar: 5.08 m

cards.term: Example: f_o = 100 cm, f_e = 1 cm. Magnifying power and angle for stars 1′ apart?
cards.definition: m = 100; the stars appear 100′ = 1.67° apart

cards.term: Exam trap: telescope in normal adjustment: distance between lenses?
cards.definition: f_o + f_e (final image at infinity); a compound microscope has an entirely different separation set by L and the eyepiece position

cards.term: NEET/JEE pattern: image of an object placed at 2f from a convex lens is seen on a screen. What if the lens is covered halfway?
cards.definition: Full image still forms, dimmer (half the light)

cards.term: Pattern: a convex lens forms real images of the same object at two positions 20 cm apart with object–screen distance 90 cm. Find f.
cards.definition: Displacement (Bessel) method: \( f = \dfrac{D^2 - d^2}{4D} = \dfrac{90^2 - 20^2}{360} \approx 21.4 \) cm (Exercise 9.19)

cards.term: Pattern: for a real image on a screen a distance D from the object, what is the maximum focal length of the lens?
cards.definition: f ≤ D/4 (at f = D/4 the two image positions coincide: u = v = 2f)

cards.term: Pattern: magnification and distances when a convex lens gives m = −2 with object at 15 cm?
cards.definition: v = mu → v = +30 cm (real); 1/f = 1/30 + 1/15 → f = 10 cm

cards.term: Pattern: lens power P in air; power in liquid of index μ_l?
cards.definition: \( P_l = P_{air}\,\dfrac{n_g/\mu_l - 1}{n_g - 1} \) (from the lens-maker relation)

cards.term: Pattern: minimum deviation D_m = A for a prism. Refractive index?
cards.definition: n = sin(A)/sin(A/2) = 2 cos(A/2); e.g. A = 60° gives n = √3

cards.term: Pattern: prism of A = 60° and n = √2. Angle of incidence for minimum deviation?
cards.definition: r = 30°, sin i = √2 × ½ → i = 45°, D_m = 2i − A = 30°

cards.term: Pattern: a ray enters a glass slab at 60° with n = √3. Angle of refraction and lateral shift for t = 3 cm?
cards.definition: sin r = sin 60°/√3 = 0.5 → r = 30°; shift = t sin(i − r)/cos r = 3 × 0.5/0.866 ≈ 1.73 cm

cards.term: Pattern: a microscope has objective f = 1 cm, eyepiece f = 5 cm. Magnifying power scales how with f_o?
cards.definition: m ∝ 1/f_o (and 1/f_e): halving f_o doubles m

cards.term: Pattern: telescope objective diameter doubled. Change in light-gathering power and resolving power?
cards.definition: Light gathered ×4 (∝ D²); resolving power ×2 (∝ D)

cards.term: Do the laws of reflection and refraction hold for curved surfaces?
cards.definition: Yes, at every point of incidence for any surface and any pair of media

cards.term: Is a real image still there when the screen is removed?
cards.definition: Yes: rays converge to the image point and diverge beyond it; the screen only diffuses them so that the image can be seen (laser shows in air)

cards.term: Why can’t you see your image in a page of a book?
cards.definition: A rough surface reflects irregularly: rays from a point do not reach one image point (diffuse instead of regular reflection)

cards.term: Why do thick lenses show coloured images?
cards.definition: Dispersion (chromatic aberration): different colours focus at different points

cards.term: Why do objects change colour under monochromatic light?
cards.definition: Colour perception depends on which constituent wavelengths are present in the incident light

cards.term: Real image on a screen (Exercise 9.1)
cards.definition: v = −54 cm, real, inverted, 5.0 cm; screen moves away as u → f

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Exercise 9.1 · candle in front of a concave mirror

Find the missing step.

Candle 2.5 cm tall at 27 cm from a concave mirror of R = 36 cm. Where should the screen be? Nature and size? What if the candle moves closer?
  1. f = −18 cm, u = −27 cm
  2. 1/v = 1/f − 1/u = −1/18 + 1/27 = −1/54 → v = −54 cm (screen 54 cm in front)
  3. ?
  4. Moving the candle closer (towards F): the screen must move farther; for u < f the image is virtual (no screen)
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Exercise 9.1 · candle in front of a concave mirror

Find the missing step.

Candle 2.5 cm tall at 27 cm from a concave mirror of R = 36 cm. Where should the screen be? Nature and size? What if the candle moves closer?
  1. f = −18 cm, u = −27 cm
  2. 1/v = 1/f − 1/u = −1/18 + 1/27 = −1/54 → v = −54 cm (screen 54 cm in front)
  3. m = −v/u = −(−54)/(−27) = −2: real, inverted, height 5.0 cm
  4. Moving the candle closer (towards F): the screen must move farther; for u < f the image is virtual (no screen)

cards.term: Exercise 9.2: 4.5 cm needle 12 cm from a convex mirror (f = 15 cm). Image and magnification?
cards.definition: 1/v = 1/15 + 1/12 → v = +6.7 cm (behind); m = −v/u = 5/9, image 2.5 cm, virtual and erect. As u → ∞, v → f and m → 0

cards.term: Exercise 9.3: tank filled to 12.5 cm appears 9.4 cm deep. n? If the liquid has n = 1.63, how far must the microscope move?
cards.definition: n = 12.5/9.4 = 1.33. New apparent depth = 12.5/1.63 = 7.67 cm; move 1.7 cm (upward)

cards.term: Exercise 9.4: given the glass–air and water–air figures, angle of refraction for a ray in water at 45° meeting glass?
Note on Exercise 9.4: is Fig 9.27(b) consistent with n_wa = 1.32?
cards.definition: With 60° in air, 1.32 needs r ≈ 41°, but the figure prints 47° (sin 60°/sin 47° = 1.18). Exams use the key’s n_wa = 1.32–1.33 and get r ≈ 38°

cards.term: Escape circle for a submerged source (Exercise 9.5)
cards.definition: Area ≈ 2.6 m²

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Exercise 9.5 · light from a bulb in a tank

Find the missing step.

Point bulb at the bottom of a tank, water depth 80 cm (n = 1.33). Area of the surface through which light emerges?
  1. Light escapes only within the cone of half-angle i_c: sin i_c = 1/1.33 = 0.75
  2. tan i_c = 0.75/√(1 − 0.5625) = 1.134
  3. Radius r = h tan i_c = 0.8 × 1.134 = 0.907 m
  4. ?
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Exercise 9.5 · light from a bulb in a tank

Find the missing step.

Point bulb at the bottom of a tank, water depth 80 cm (n = 1.33). Area of the surface through which light emerges?
  1. Light escapes only within the cone of half-angle i_c: sin i_c = 1/1.33 = 0.75
  2. tan i_c = 0.75/√(1 − 0.5625) = 1.134
  3. Radius r = h tan i_c = 0.8 × 1.134 = 0.907 m
  4. Area = πr² = 2.6 m²

cards.term: Exercise 9.6: D_m = 40° for a 60° prism. n? In water (1.33), new D_m?
cards.definition: n = sin 50°/sin 30° = 1.53. In water: n_gw = 1.15; sin((60 + D)/2) = 1.15 × 0.5 → D ≈ 10°

cards.term: Exercise 9.7: double-convex lens, both faces the same R, n = 1.55, f = 20 cm. R?
Exercise 9.8: a convergent beam meets at P; a lens is placed 12 cm before P. Where does it converge for (a) f = +20 cm (b) f = −16 cm?
cards.definition: Object is virtual: u = +12 cm. (a) 1/v = 1/20 + 1/12 → v = 7.5 cm (real, right). (b) 1/v = −1/16 + 1/12 → v = 48 cm (real, right)

cards.term: Exercise 9.9: 3.0 cm object 14 cm from a concave lens (f = −21 cm). Image? As the object moves away?
cards.definition: 1/v = −1/21 − 1/14 → v = −8.4 cm, m = 0.6: virtual, erect, 1.8 cm. As u → ∞, v → f (never beyond); at u = f the image is at 10.5 cm, not at infinity

cards.term:
Exercise 9.11: compound microscope f_o = 2.0 cm, f_e = 6.25 cm, lenses 15 cm apart. Object distance and magnifying power for image at
(a) 25 cm
(b) infinity?
cards.definition: (a) u_e = −5 cm, v_o = 10 cm, u_o = −2.5 cm, m = (10/2.5)(1 + 25/6.25) = 20. (b) v_o = 8.75, u_o = −2.59 cm, m = 3.38 × 4 = 13.5

cards.term: Exercise 9.12: f_o = 8.0 mm, f_e = 2.5 cm, object at 9.0 mm from the objective, normal eye. Separation and magnifying power?
cards.definition: v_o = 7.2 cm; eyepiece object distance 2.27 cm: separation 9.47 cm; m = (7.2/0.9)(1 + 25/2.5) = 88

cards.term: Exercise 9.13: f_o = 144 cm, f_e = 6.0 cm. Magnifying power and separation?
cards.definition: m = 144/6 = 24; separation f_o + f_e = 150 cm

cards.term:
Exercise 9.14: refractor with f_o = 15 m, f_e = 1.0 cm.
(a) m
(b) diameter of the Moon’s image formed by the objective?
cards.definition: (a) m = 1500. (b) Moon subtends 3.48 × 10⁶/3.8 × 10⁸ = 9.16 × 10⁻³ rad; image diameter = 15 × 9.16 × 10⁻³ = 13.7 cm

cards.term: Exercise 9.15: use the mirror equation to show a convex mirror always gives a virtual, diminished image between F and P.
cards.definition: f > 0, u < 0: 1/v = 1/f − 1/u > 0, so v > 0 (virtual). v = fu/(u − f): |v| < f, so image lies between P and F; m = f/(f − u) < 1: diminished

cards.term: Exercise 9.15(a),(d): concave mirror properties from the equation?
cards.definition: (a) f < 0, u < 0 with |f| < |u| < 2|f|: v = fu/(u − f) has |v| > 2|f|, real and beyond C. (d) f < u < 0 (object inside F): u − f > 0 so v > 0: virtual, and m = f/(f − u) = > 1: enlarged

cards.term: Exercise 9.16: pin viewed from 50 cm above through a 15 cm glass slab (n = 1.5). Apparent raise? Depends on slab position?
cards.definition: Shift = t(1 − 1/n) = 15 × (1/3) = 5 cm. Independent of where the slab is (for small angles)

cards.term: Exercise 9.17(a): light pipe, core n = 1.68, cladding 1.44. Range of incidence angles that get totally reflected?
cards.definition: sin i′_c = 1.44/1.68 → i′_c = 59°; r_max = 31°; sin i_max = 1.68 sin 31° → 0 < i < 60°

cards.term: Exercise 9.17(b): with no cladding (n = 1.68 in air)?
cards.definition: i′_c = sin⁻¹(1/1.68) = 36.5°. Even i = 90° gives r = 36.5°, i′ = 53.5° > i′_c, so all rays (0–90°) are totally reflected

cards.term: Exercise 9.18: image of a bulb on the opposite wall, 3 m away, by a convex lens. Maximum focal length?
cards.definition: Real image needs D ≥ 4f, so f_max = 0.75 m

cards.term: Exercise 9.19: object–screen 90 cm, two lens positions 20 cm apart. f?
cards.definition: f = (D² − d²)/4D = (8100 − 400)/360 = 21.4 cm

cards.term: Two lenses 8 cm apart (Exercise 9.20)
cards.definition: Side-dependent; m = 0.652; image 0.98 cm

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Exercise 9.20 · separated lenses

Find the missing step.

The 30 cm convex and 20 cm concave lenses are 8.0 cm apart. Effective focal length? Does it depend on the side of incidence? Magnification for a 1.5 cm object 40 cm from the convex lens?
  1. Parallel beam from the convex side: v₁ = +30, then u₂ = +22 (virtual object): v₂ = −220 cm
  2. From the concave side: v₁ = −20, u₂ = −28: v₂ = −420 cm (different!)
  3. So the notion of effective focal length is not useful here (depends on the side)
  4. ?
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Exercise 9.20 · separated lenses

Find the missing step.

The 30 cm convex and 20 cm concave lenses are 8.0 cm apart. Effective focal length? Does it depend on the side of incidence? Magnification for a 1.5 cm object 40 cm from the convex lens?
  1. Parallel beam from the convex side: v₁ = +30, then u₂ = +22 (virtual object): v₂ = −220 cm
  2. From the concave side: v₁ = −20, u₂ = −28: v₂ = −420 cm (different!)
  3. So the notion of effective focal length is not useful here (depends on the side)
  4. Object 40 cm: v₁ = 120 (m₁ = 3); u₂ = +112, v₂ = −92 (m₂ = 20/92); m = 0.652, image size 0.98 cm

cards.term: Exercise 9.22: card of 1 mm² squares viewed through a magnifier held close to the eye, card at 9 cm. Magnification, area of each square, magnifying power?
cards.definition: Key: 1/v − 1/u with v = −90 cm gives m = 10, area = 10 × 10 × 1 mm² = 1 cm², magnifying power = 25/9 = 2.8. They differ: m = |v/u| but MP = 25/|u|; equal only when the image is at 25 cm

cards.term: Correction: Exercise 9.22 says f = 9 cm and the card is at 9 cm. Does the key match?
cards.definition: No: the printed question says f = 9 cm, but the key’s v = −90 cm only works with f = 10 cm (u = −9 cm). With f = 9 cm and u = 9 cm the image would be at infinity. The key’s numbers come from an older f = 10 cm version; the concept (m ≠ MP) is what is examined

cards.term: Exercise 9.23: viewing the squares distinctly with maximum magnifying power. Where to hold the lens? m? Is m = MP?
cards.definition: Image at 25 cm. Key (f = 10 cm): u = −7.14 cm, m = 3.5, and yes m = MP when the image is at the near point. Recomputed with f = 9 cm: u = −6.6 cm, m = 1 + 25/9 = 3.8

cards.term: Exercise 9.24: how far should the card be to get a virtual square area of 6.25 mm² (m = 2.5)? Seen distinctly?
cards.definition: Key: u = −6 cm, |v| = 15 cm (f = 10 cm). With f = 9 cm: u = −5.4 cm, |v| = 13.5 cm. Either way the image is closer than 25 cm, so the eye cannot see it distinctly

cards.term: Exercise 9.25(a),(b): magnifier: angle of object = angle of image, so in what sense does it magnify? Effect of moving the eye back?
cards.definition: (a) The object can be placed much closer than 25 cm, at a larger angle than at D. (b) Angular magnification decreases slightly as the angle subtended at the eye falls

cards.term: Exercise 9.25(c): why can’t we keep reducing the focal length of a simple lens to get more magnifying power?
cards.definition: Grinding very short f lenses is hard, and spherical and chromatic aberrations grow; a simple lens is limited to about 3× (aberration-corrected systems reach 10× more)

cards.term: Design for 30× (Exercise 9.26)
cards.definition: Object 1.5 cm from objective; lenses 11.67 cm apart

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Exercise 9.26 · setting up a compound microscope

Find the missing step.

Angular magnification 30× with f_o = 1.25 cm and f_e = 5 cm (image at 25 cm). How to set up the microscope?
  1. Eyepiece magnification: 1 + 25/5 = 6, so objective m_o = 30/6 = 5
  2. ?
  3. Eyepiece image at 25 cm: 1/u_e = −1/25 − 1/5 → |u_e| = 4.17 cm
  4. Separation = 7.5 + 4.17 = 11.67 cm; object 1.5 cm from the objective
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Exercise 9.26 · setting up a compound microscope

Find the missing step.

Angular magnification 30× with f_o = 1.25 cm and f_e = 5 cm (image at 25 cm). How to set up the microscope?
  1. Eyepiece magnification: 1 + 25/5 = 6, so objective m_o = 30/6 = 5
  2. v_o/|u_o| = 5 and 1/v_o − 1/u_o = 1/1.25 → u_o = −1.5 cm, v_o = 7.5 cm
  3. Eyepiece image at 25 cm: 1/u_e = −1/25 − 1/5 → |u_e| = 4.17 cm
  4. Separation = 7.5 + 4.17 = 11.67 cm; object 1.5 cm from the objective

cards.term: Exercise 9.27: telescope with f_o = 140 cm, f_e = 5.0 cm. m for (a) normal adjustment (b) final image at 25 cm?
cards.definition: (a) m = 140/5 = 28. (b) m = (140/5)(1 + 5/25) = 33.6

cards.term: Exercise 9.28: same telescope on a 100 m tower 3 km away: separation? Image height by the objective and final image height at 25 cm?
cards.definition: Separation 145 cm. Angle = 1/30 rad → objective image = 140/30 = 4.7 cm; eyepiece magnification 6 → final image ≈ 28 cm

cards.term: Exercise 9.29: Cassegrain with mirrors 20 mm apart, R = 220 mm (primary), 140 mm (secondary). Final image of a far object?
cards.definition: Primary f = 110 mm; image would form 90 mm beyond the secondary (virtual object). Secondary f = 70 mm: 1/v = 1/70 − 1/90 → v = 315 mm from the secondary

cards.term: Exercise 9.30: mirror on a galvanometer coil deflects 3.5°. Shift of the reflected spot on a screen 1.5 m away?
cards.definition: Reflected ray turns by 2θ = 7°: d = 1.5 tan 7° = 18.4 cm

cards.term: Exercise 9.31: needle over a convex lens (n = 1.50) on a liquid layer on a plane mirror: image at needle position at 45.0 cm; without liquid at 30.0 cm. n_liquid?
cards.definition: Without liquid f = 30 cm, so R = 30 cm (biconvex). With liquid: 1/45 = 1/30 + 1/f_liq → f_liq = −90 cm (plano-concave liquid lens: −(n − 1)/30). So n − 1 = 1/3: n = 1.33

cards.term: Chapter 9 formula sheet
cards.definition: Mirror equation: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f, f = R/2; Mirror magnification: m = −v/u; Snell’s law: sin i/sin r = n₂₁ = n₂/n₁; Critical angle: sin i_c = n₂/n₁ (n₁ > n₂); Spherical surface: n₂/v − n₁/u = (n₂ − n₁)/R; Lens formula: 1/v − 1/u = 1/f; Lens maker: 1/f = (n − 1)(1/R₁ − 1/R₂); Lens power, contact: P = 1/f; P = P₁ + P₂; Prism: n = sin[(A + D_m)/2]/sin(A/2); δ = (n − 1)A; Simple microscope: m = 1 + D/f (near), D/f (∞); Compound microscope: m = (L/f_o)(D/f_e); Telescope: m = f_o/f_e; length f_o + f_e

cards.term: Chapter 9 concept checks
cards.definition: A convex mirror can form a real image of a real object: False (always virtual); Frequency changes when light enters glass: False (λ and v change); TIR needs light going from a denser to a rarer medium: True; A glass lens in water has a longer focal length than in air: True; Compound microscope: objective has the smaller focal length: True; Refracting telescope objective has a small aperture: False (large)
